docs.title: Air Quality and Bioinformatics
docs.text:
A professional development course for science teachers

Welcome. This course invites you to investigate air quality in your own community alongside your students, and to connect what you find to human biology and health. You will work with low cost sensors, analyze the data you collect, and design classroom activities that fit your curriculum and your students.

The course is built around discussion. In each unit you will write your own thinking first, then read and respond to colleagues. Your experience in your own classroom is the material this course works with.

docs.title: How the course is organized
docs.text:
Each module contains short readings, videos, and an activity. Activities link to a discussion thread where the whole cohort writes together. There are no quizzes and no grades. You set your own pace.

  • Module 1. Getting started

    Tools, sensors, and how we will work together.

    Available soon

  • Module 2. Science education for society

    What kind of science education do we need, and what does that mean for our classrooms.

    3 units

  • Module 3. Air quality and health

    Particulate matter, exposure, and respiratory conditions such as asthma.

    Available soon

  • Module 4. Working with data

    Collecting, cleaning, and interpreting sensor data with students.

    Available soon

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Set up your discussion access

Discussion happens in our course repository. If you have not yet accepted the invitation, check the email address you gave us for a message from GitHub. Once you accept, you will be able to read and post in every discussion thread.

Open the discussion board :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Module 2. Science Education for Society
docs.text: This module asks you to step back from the day to day of teaching and name what you think science education is for. We start with your own beliefs, then look at two ways scholars have described the purpose of scientific literacy, then return to your classroom.

docs.title: Units in this module
docs.text: Unit Title What you will do 2.1.1 Your beliefs about science education Write about your own beliefs, respond to colleagues, watch two short videos 2.1.2 Vision 1 and Vision 2 in practice Examine classroom examples and sort them (available soon) 2.1.3 Your curriculum, your context Map one of your existing units onto the two visions (available soon)

docs.title: Time
docs.text: About 90 minutes, which you can spread across the week. The discussion stays open, so you can return to it after others have posted.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Your beliefs about science education
docs.text: When you were first learning how to teach, you may have been asked about the kind of science education we need in society and how that can be fostered in a classroom. Or, you may have asked this question to yourself over the years as you have designed curricular experiences for your students.

docs.title: :material-forum: Discussion: Beliefs about science education
docs.text:
Write before you read

What kind of science education do we need in society, and how do you foster this in your classroom?

Write your thoughts in the discussion forum. After you have written your own thoughts, read and comment on the thoughts of at least 3 other course participants.

Please use these guidelines for constructive feedback when you respond.

Go to the discussion thread :material-arrow-right:

Come back to this page once you have posted.

docs.title: Two short videos
docs.text:
Hopefully, you will have read a number of different ideas about the kind of science education we need in society, and you will have learned different ways that this is fostered in the classroom from other course participants.

These next two short videos offer some ideas that you may or may not have already thought about. They are by the scientist and author Dr. Brian Greene, a well known American theoretical physicist and professor at Columbia University. You can read more about him here.

Fostering public engagementFostering excitement in school

docs.title: Two visions of scientific literacy
docs.text:
Let's review Brian Greene's words in the last video.

[Science] is fantastic material. This is material to die for. And yet, if it is taught in a way that we usually teach it, where we focus in so quickly on the details in order to be able to get kids to solve the equation, know the parts of the cell, balance the reaction, without a commensurate focus on the big wondrous ideas, the ideas that get us up in the morning and want us to go to work, what we do is we leave science lifeless. And what we do is we create another generation that goes out into the world and basically thinks, 'science is just a subject in school. It's best left to the scientists. It's material that I can simply leave behind when I cross the threshold of the science lab for the last time.' And that is the vital thing that we need to change.

He has outlined two ways to think about the kind of science education we need in society. Some science education scholars have termed these Vision 1 and Vision 2 scientific literacy.

While we are certainly interested in developing both Vision 1 and Vision 2 scientific literacy, in this course we offer curriculum and pedagogies that are aimed at engaging all learners who may become scientists or intelligent consumers of scientific knowledge and products, so that they will be able to use science to improve their lives.

Before you move on

  • [ ] You posted your own thinking in the discussion
  • [ ] You responded to at least 3 colleagues
  • [ ] You watched both videos

Next up: 2.1.2 Vision 1 and Vision 2 in practice

docs.title: Vision 1
docs.text:
An education that promotes knowledge and skills that aim to produce scientists.

That knowledge might require students to know the parts of the cell, or the skill of solving the equation and balancing the reaction.

docs.title: Vision 2
docs.text:
An education that promotes the interest and application of science in everyday life, regardless of whether one becomes a scientist.

It gets students to pay attention to the products of science and enables them to evaluate those products in light of their own circumstances, such as whether they are genetically or environmentally at higher risk of contracting a disease, and then to apply steps to mitigate that risk.
